title: A day of virtue
hookLine: five precepts become eight for one day, and every sense notices.
tomorrow: is letting go a loss, or something else?

cards: Some people take one day a week away from screens, just to hear themselves think. The Buddha's lay followers had an older version, and it reached every sense.
So what changes when you keep eight precepts for a day instead of five? Your mouth notices by mid-afternoon. Your ears notice when nothing's playing.

teach.h: FOR ONE DAY AND NIGHT, AS THEY DO.
teach.b: In the Anguttara Nikaya the Buddha describes the observance day, the uposatha.
The arahants, the fully awakened, keep these precepts all their lives, he says, and a lay follower can say: for this one day and night, I'll do as they do. So the five become eight.
The third tightens: for the day, no sexual activity at all. Then three are added, and each one is a sense.

Taste: no food after midday. Hearing and sight: no dancing, singing, music or shows, and with them no garlands, perfumes or makeup, nothing worn to be looked at. Touch: no high, luxurious bed; you sleep low and plain.
Read the list as a body would. The tongue gets a quiet afternoon. The ears get silence.
The skin gets a plain mat. Nothing on it is harsh, and nothing in it is a punishment.
It's a day with the volume turned down, so you can hear what's left when nothing is added.
That's why it's called a clean day. Not scrubbed, just uncluttered. At temples, people may come on those days, dressed simply, to keep the eight together.

how: On uposatha days, set by the phases of the moon, Theravada lay Buddhists may go to the temple, sometimes dressed in white, to take the eight precepts for a day and night, listen to teaching and meditate.

games.q: what does “a day of virtue” mean?
o: a holiday when temples hold a feast and a parade
eight precepts kept for a day, with every sense at rest
a day of silence kept once a year by monks

games.q: the eight, by sense — tap the pairs.

s: the eight precepts are only for monks and nuns
the Buddha describes lay followers keeping them for one day and night, as the awakened keep them for life.
no food after midday is one of the eight
it's one of the three added precepts, the one the tongue notices first.
the third precept stays exactly as it is in the five
for the day it tightens: no sexual activity at all.

games.q: you're keeping the eight for a day, and a friend invites you to a movie night at six. which precept does that bump into?
o: no dancing, singing, music or shows.
games.why: the seventh precept covers shows and music. the eight turn the volume down for one day, so a quiet evening fits it.

practice: Sit on the floor, or on a plain chair, with nothing playing. For the whole sit, let each sense go plain: no taste in the mouth, no music in the ears, nothing to look at but what's already in front of you.
Notice what's still here when nothing is added.

wordCard.voice: A day of virtue: the eight precepts kept for one day and night, the way the awakened keep them for life. Every sense gets a rest.

orig.note: Pali: the observance day, when lay followers may keep the eight precepts.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: a clean day, with every sense uncluttered rather than scrubbed. Until next time.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 8.41 (the uposatha with eight factors: as long as they live the arahants abstain from killing, stealing, unchastity, false speech, intoxicants, eating at the wrong time, dancing, singing, music and shows, garlands, scents and adornment, and high and luxurious beds; 'I too, for this night and day' follow them)
